summary: This informational document registers the application/pkcs8-encrypted media type for the PKCS #8 EncryptedPrivateKeyInfo type. A file or message of this type carries a single encrypted private key, BER-encoded. Registration helps software identify such data consistently.

eli5.summary: A locked box needs a label saying 'locked key inside.' This registers the official label for a file holding one encrypted secret key.

questions: what is the application/pkcs8-encrypted media type
how to label an encrypted private key file
how to handle password encoding in pkcs8
subtitle: Register the official MIME type for encrypted private key files.

tldr.problem: PKCS #8 is a widely used format for storing private cryptographic keys, often encrypted with a password. Software and file systems need a standard way to identify these encrypted files so they can be processed correctly.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC registers the MIME media type application/pkcs8-encrypted with IANA (the Internet Assigned Numbers Authority). It specifies how the media type should be used, what password-mapping methods are supported, and what file extensions to use.
tldr.outcome: Software can now consistently recognize and handle encrypted PKCS #8 private key files using the standard MIME type, improving interoperability and reducing misidentification.

today: RFC 8351 is an Informational RFC from the Independent Submission stream, published in June 2018. The media type has been registered with IANA and is now available for use in email headers, HTTP Content-Type fields, and other contexts where MIME types are needed to identify encrypted PKCS #8 private key files.

sections.title: What Is Being Registered
sections.content:
PKCS #8 is a standard format (originally from RSA Laboratories) for encoding cryptographic private keys. When a private key is sensitive, it is typically encrypted with a password using a password-based encryption scheme, producing what is called an EncryptedPrivateKeyInfo structure.

This RFC registers the MIME media type (also called a content type) application/pkcs8-encrypted to identify files and messages that contain a single encrypted PKCS #8 private key in BER-encoded form. The registration allows software to recognize such files by their MIME type, similar to how application/json identifies JSON files or image/png identifies PNG images.

PKCS #8 is widely supported by cryptographic software stacks on all modern operating systems. Registering a standard MIME type makes it easier for tools to identify, import, export, and exercise private keys consistently.
sections.eli5: PKCS #8 is a way to store secret keys in a file. This registers an official label for those files so programs know what they are.

sections.title: Media Type Details
sections.content:
The registration specifies several attributes:

Type and subtype: application/pkcs8-encrypted. The 'application' type means this is binary application data; 'pkcs8-encrypted' specifies the format.

Encoding: Binary. The data is BER-encoded (a binary encoding scheme for structured data), not text.

Password mapping parameter: An optional parameter that specifies which character encoding to use when converting a password (which a user might type as text) to the octets needed for decryption. This is important for interoperability when the file creator used a different character encoding (like Shift-JIS) than the person decrypting it (who might use UTF-8). Special values like *pkcs12, *precis, *hex, and *dtmf handle common cases.

File extension: .p8e is recommended for files containing an encrypted PKCS #8 private key.

Interoperability: PKCS #8 is simpler to implement than PKCS #12 (which can hold multiple keys and certificates together) and is widely recognized across cryptographic libraries.
sections.eli5: The label says 'this is an encrypted key file,' what encoding it used, and whether the password might be in a non-English format.

sections.title: Security Implications
sections.content:
Because PKCS #8 files contain private keys, they carry significant security implications:

Confidentiality: An encrypted PKCS #8 file is only secure if the password is strong. Weak passwords, poor algorithm choices, or insufficient salting (adding random data during encryption) can make the private key vulnerable to attack.

Password handling: The password-mapping parameter is not cryptographically protected, so recipients cannot rely on it as the only way to decrypt a file. If the mapping fails, they may need to try other encodings to recover the key.

Simplicity advantage: Unlike PKCS #12, which can contain multiple objects and certificates, PKCS #8 contains exactly one private key (and optionally key attributes). This simplicity reduces the risk of accidentally including unintended secrets.
sections.eli5: A locked key file is only safe if the password is good. The file format itself is simple and reduces the risk of accidentally including the wrong secrets.

sections.title: Implementation and Use
sections.content:
PKCS #8 is widely supported by cryptographic toolkits and libraries across platforms. Applications that need to import, export, or use encrypted private keys can rely on standard PKCS #8 support.

The media type registration allows tools to automatically recognize encrypted PKCS #8 files by their Content-Type header (in email or HTTP), file extension, or MIME type declaration. This enables seamless interoperability between different security applications.

When a user provides a password to decrypt an encrypted PKCS #8 file, the application uses that password with the specified encryption algorithm to unlock the private key. The optional password-mapping parameter helps bridge different character encodings when legacy systems are involved.
sections.eli5: Programs can now recognize and use encrypted key files automatically by looking at their type label instead of guessing.
